newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX Board agrees to change foreign crude rules.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX Board agrees to change foreign crude rules.

text.p: The New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) Board has agreed to change its rules for delivering foreign crude against oil futures contracts, a NYMEX spokesperson said on Thursday.
The decision, reached on Wednesday evening, is aimed at more evenly distributing often-unwanted imported crude among futures buyers who hold their contracts to maturity.
The board met to discuss alternative arrangements after several months of exceptionally heavy delivery of foreign crude, which caused problems for some refiners.
The NYMEX spokesperson said the Board agreed to change the delivery system so that distribution of foreign crude is more proportionate.

Problems surfaced in April when a record 2.73 million barrels of Nigerian Bonny Light, North Sea Brent and Norwegian Oseberg were delivered against the May contract. The problems continuted with the June and July contracts.
These were the first foreign crude deliveries into the exchange since 1992.

The Board's action came in response to recommendations made by the Crude Oil Advisory Committee, which met on Tuesday to discuss the issue. The committee, which is comprised of representatives of more than 20 private oil companies, reviewed the foreign grades that are currently deliverable and recommended maintaining the present system with some changes.

Some U.S. refiners have complained that the recent pattern of large foreign deliveries unfairly burdens them with unfamiliar grades that aren't easily fed into their refineries, which usually run domestic crudes.

Brent, Forties and Oseberg from the North Sea, Bonny Light and Colombian Cusiana crudes are currently deliverable against the contract, with premiums or discounts to the settlement price based on crude quality.

Under the new rules, buyers who prefer to receive foreign crude would still be matched with sellers first. For any remaining foreign crude, buyers preferring domestic barrels would each receive foreign crude in proportion to their overall position. Buyers of less than 60,000 barrels would be excluded.
Under the current system, the NYMEX distributes foreign crude in parcels of 80,000 barrels among buyers who prefer domestic grades, beginning with the largest buyers.
Under a new ratability rule, sellers of multiple foreign grades would have to supply each grade at the start of the month.

The current system allows sellers to start the month with one grade and switch to another grade later in the month. That vexed some refiners who usually blend the foreign crudes with domestic grades to make them more digestible for their plants.
"A refiner was delivered Bonny Light, but Brent showed up in the middle of the month," a Midcontinent refiner said. "A refiner needs to know how to plan."
The committee also agreed to set up a subcommittee to analyze the current price differentials and explore the possibility of adjusting them more frequently.
That move was targeted mainly at Bonny Light, whose API gravity has deteriorated from a 1995 average of 35.7 degrees to 34.7 degrees in the first four months of 1997.
The committee turned down a NYMEX staff recommendation that Bonny Light be eliminated from the list of deliverable crudes. That left some U.S. refiners warning of further problems to come.

"The reason there was a problem is that some buyers didn't want the crude or figured that the crude didn't have the value that the Merc said it did. That problem still has to be addressed," said a U.S. refiner.
"The Bonny Light should be excluded. There's too big a variance with domestic crudes," he said. "Until they do that, there's going to continue to be problems."
Bonny Light now fetches a premium of 40 cents a barrel.
Several other refiners, however, favor the liquidity foreign crudes bring to the current system.
"It's a fairly robust system in that it has a mechanism to adjust for foreign crudes," a Gulf Coast refiner said. "I think the system as a whole has worked the way it's supposed to work."
Indeed, the tapering off of foreign deliveries in July suggests that the market eventually absorbs the barrels, some refiners say.
The rule changes will now be submitted to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) for final approval and should take effect in a few months, the spokesperson said.
--New York Energy Desk ((+1 212 859 1620))
